def: Death of intestinal wall tissue in premature or very sick newborns, often after feeding starts, causing bloating, bloody stool and gas within the bowel wall (pneumatosis intestinalis). Can lead to perforation.

A dimorphic fungus found in soil with bird and bat droppings in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys. Inhaled spores are engulfed by macrophages, causing pulmonary disease and, in some patients, disseminated infection.
A protein of synaptic vesicle membranes used as an immunohistochemical marker of neuroendocrine differentiation, positive in small cell carcinoma, carcinoid tumors and neuroblastoma.
Restricting movement of a body part with a splint, cast or bed rest. Prolonged immobility promotes venous stasis (deep vein thrombosis), muscle atrophy, bone loss and pressure ulcers.
A sulfur-containing amino acid made from methionine and recycled back using folate, B12 or converted to cysteine using B6. High levels cause endothelial injury and thrombosis, as in homocystinuria.

Compounds in insecticides and nerve agents that irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing excess acetylcholine (salivation, lacrimation, diarrhea, miosis, bronchospasm). Treated with atropine and pralidoxime.
Magnesium ammonium phosphate crystals forming kidney stones in alkaline urine infected by urease-producing bacteria such as Proteus. Can grow into large staghorn calculi.
Abnormally high blood ammonia, from urea cycle defects or liver failure. Causes lethargy, vomiting, asterixis and cerebral edema, and can progress to coma.
Enzymes (ALT and AST) that transfer amino groups between amino acids and keto acids using pyridoxal phosphate. Released from damaged hepatocytes, so elevated serum levels signal liver injury.
Paralysis or weakness of the eye muscles, limiting eye movements. Seen in cranial nerve III, IV or VI lesions, internuclear ophthalmoplegia, and Wernicke encephalopathy.
Pathologic loss of memory, either for events after an insult (anterograde) or before it (retrograde). Causes include hippocampal or thalamic damage, thiamine deficiency and psychological trauma.
An atypical antidepressant that blocks alpha-2 autoreceptors and 5-HT2 and 5-HT3 receptors. Side effects are sedation, increased appetite and weight gain.
The three membranes covering the brain and spinal cord: dura mater, arachnoid and pia mater. Inflamed in meningitis.
The S-shaped part of the large intestine between the descending colon and rectum. A common site of diverticulosis, volvulus and colorectal cancer.
Incomplete closure of the neural tube or vertebral arches, as in spina bifida occulta, meningocele and myelomeningocele. Linked to folate deficiency and elevated alpha-fetoprotein.

Non-enveloped, single-stranded RNA viruses of the picornavirus family, including poliovirus, coxsackieviruses and echoviruses, spread by the fecal-oral route. Cause aseptic meningitis, myocarditis and hand-foot-mouth disease.
Round intracytoplasmic inclusions of aggregated alpha-synuclein in neurons. Characteristic of Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia.

Congenital absence of enteric ganglion cells in the distal bowel (neural crest migration failure, often RET mutation), so the segment stays contracted. Causes delayed meconium passage and a dilated proximal colon.
A procedure where an endoscope is passed to the duodenum and contrast is injected into the bile and pancreatic ducts. Used to image and treat stones, strictures and tumors; can cause pancreatitis.
A break in the skull bones. Temporal bone fractures can tear the middle meningeal artery, causing epidural hematoma; basilar fractures cause raccoon eyes, Battle sign and CSF leak.

Compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots below the spinal cord end, causing saddle anesthesia, bladder and bowel dysfunction and leg weakness. A surgical emergency, often from a massive disc herniation.
The seven vertebrae of the neck (C1-C7). C1 (atlas) and C2 (axis) are specialized for head rotation and nodding.

Excessive, hard-to-control worry about multiple everyday matters lasting at least 6 months, with restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration and muscle tension. First-line treatment is SSRIs/SNRIs and CBT.

An antidepressant and smoking-cessation aid that inhibits norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake. Lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated in bulimia and seizure disorders; lacks sexual side effects.
An atypical (second-generation) antipsychotic that blocks dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, with strong histamine blockade causing sedation and weight gain. Also used in bipolar disorder.
The main component of the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria; its lipid A portion is endotoxin, which activates TLR4 and can trigger septic shock.

The most common primary malignant bone tumor, arising in adolescents at the metaphysis near the knee. X-ray shows a sunburst pattern and Codman triangle; associated with Paget disease and retinoblastoma (RB) mutations.
A poxvirus skin infection producing small, flesh-colored, dome-shaped papules with central dimpling (umbilication). Spreads by direct contact and is self-limited in healthy children.

A beta-lactamase enzyme produced by some bacteria (such as Staphylococcus aureus) that cleaves the beta-lactam ring of penicillins, making them ineffective. Resisted by methicillin, nafcillin and oxacillin.

A curved, urease-producing gram-negative rod that colonizes the stomach, causing gastritis, peptic ulcers, gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma. Treated with a proton pump inhibitor plus antibiotics.
A genus of curved gram-negative rods that live in the stomach and intestine; the major human pathogen is H. pylori, which causes gastritis and ulcers.
A club-shaped gram-positive rod that causes diphtheria by producing an exotoxin that inactivates elongation factor 2. Causes a gray pseudomembrane in the throat and myocarditis.

Infection by HPV, a DNA virus that infects skin and mucosa. Low-risk types 6 and 11 cause warts; high-risk types 16 and 18 cause cervical, anal and oropharyngeal cancer by E6 and E7 inactivating p53 and Rb.
Inflammation of the retina, often infectious. Cytomegalovirus retinitis in AIDS gives a pizza-pie (hemorrhage and necrosis) fundus and visual loss.
A highly aggressive B-cell lymphoma with t(8;14) translocation activating MYC. Histology shows a starry-sky pattern; endemic form in Africa is EBV-linked and presents as a jaw mass.
Inflammation of the prostate, often bacterial (E. coli), causing dysuria, pelvic pain and a tender boggy prostate. Acute cases may be febrile; chronic cases cause recurrent UTIs.
Excessive bleeding after delivery (over 500 mL vaginal or 1000 mL cesarean). The most common cause is uterine atony; others are retained placenta, lacerations and coagulopathy.
A girl's first menstrual period, typically around age 12 to 13, following thelarche. Marks the onset of ovulatory cycles.
Excessive thoughts, feelings and behaviors about one or more physical symptoms, lasting over 6 months, whether or not a medical cause is found. Not intentionally produced.
Drugs that prevent or relieve nausea and vomiting, including 5-HT3 blockers (ondansetron), dopamine blockers, antihistamines and NK1 antagonists.
Sexual drive or desire. Decreased by depression, hypogonadism and many drugs (SSRIs, antipsychotics); increased by testosterone and dopaminergic drugs.
Coordinated waves of smooth muscle contraction and relaxation that propel contents along the GI tract, controlled by the enteric nervous system.
The herpesvirus that causes Kaposi sarcoma, primary effusion lymphoma and Castleman disease, mainly in immunocompromised patients such as those with AIDS.
An enzyme that cleaves phospholipids. Clostridium perfringens alpha toxin is a lecithinase (phospholipase C) causing gas gangrene; pancreatic phospholipase A2 digests dietary phospholipids.
G-protein-coupled receptors for ADH: V1 on vascular smooth muscle causes vasoconstriction (Gq), and V2 on collecting duct cells inserts aquaporin-2 water channels (Gs, raising cAMP).

A large iodinated glycoprotein in thyroid follicles that serves as the scaffold for thyroid hormone synthesis and storage. Serum levels are used as a tumor marker for thyroid cancer after thyroidectomy.
A G-protein-coupled receptor on thyroid follicular cells that stimulates thyroid hormone production through Gs. Activating antibodies cause Graves disease.
Development of male characteristics in a female, such as hirsutism, deepened voice, clitoromegaly and acne, due to excess androgens (e.g., congenital adrenal hyperplasia, androgen-secreting tumors).
Excessive thirst and fluid intake, seen in uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus and primary psychogenic polydipsia.
Elevated blood cholesterol, especially LDL. Familial hypercholesterolemia is caused by LDL receptor defects and causes tendon xanthomas and early coronary disease.
Mutated or overexpressed genes that promote cell growth and cancer (e.g., RAS, MYC, HER2). The normal version is called a proto-oncogene.
Insulin deficiency caused by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, usually presenting in youth with polyuria, weight loss and diabetic ketoacidosis. Associated with HLA-DR3 and DR4.
Thickening of small arteriole walls. Hyaline type (benign hypertension, diabetes) shows pink protein deposits; hyperplastic type (malignant hypertension) shows onion-skin lamination.
The characteristic facial appearance associated with a particular condition, such as the moon face of Cushing syndrome or the flat facies of Down syndrome.
The external female genitalia, including the labia, clitoris and vestibule.
A virus whose genome is DNA. Most are double-stranded (herpes, adeno, pox, HPV); exceptions are parvovirus B19 (single-stranded) and hepatitis B (partially double-stranded).
A paramyxovirus infection causing painful parotid swelling, plus orchitis, aseptic meningitis and pancreatitis. Prevented by the MMR vaccine.
Skin glands that secrete sweat: eccrine glands (widespread, cooling, cholinergic sympathetic innervation) and apocrine glands (axilla and groin, after puberty).
The armpit, containing axillary lymph nodes, the brachial plexus and the axillary artery and vein.

The most common inherited bleeding disorder, from deficient or defective von Willebrand factor, which carries factor VIII and mediates platelet adhesion. Causes mucosal bleeding with prolonged bleeding time; treated with desmopressin.
Positively charged proteins rich in lysine and arginine around which DNA winds to form nucleosomes. Acetylation opens chromatin, while methylation often silences genes.
A basic, positively charged essential amino acid abundant in histones. Hydroxylated in collagen synthesis; acetylation and methylation of its residues regulate gene expression.
An acidic, negatively charged amino acid that serves in the urea cycle, purine/pyrimidine synthesis and the malate-aspartate shuttle.
A sequence of three mRNA nucleotides that specifies one amino acid or a stop signal during translation.
An enzyme that cuts nucleic acid chains within the strand rather than at the ends. Restriction enzymes and DNA repair enzymes are examples.

The most common lysosomal storage disease, from glucocerebrosidase deficiency, causing glucocerebroside buildup in macrophages. Features hepatosplenomegaly, bone pain and crumpled-tissue-paper cells; treated with enzyme replacement.

Autosomal dominant condition from germline DNA mismatch repair gene mutations (MLH1, MSH2), causing microsatellite instability and early colorectal, endometrial and other cancers, without numerous polyps.
Shrinkage of muscle from disuse, denervation or disease. Denervation atrophy is more severe and involves fasciculations.
Autosomal recessive defect (most often cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency) causing homocysteine buildup, with lens dislocation downward, marfanoid habitus, thromboses and intellectual disability.
Chest pain from myocardial ischemia that occurs at rest or is new or worsening, without troponin elevation. Caused by a ruptured plaque with partial thrombus.
The molecular motor protein of thick filaments in muscle; its heads bind actin, hydrolyze ATP and produce force through cross-bridge cycling.
The phase of the cardiac cycle when ventricles contract and eject blood.
Sensory receptors that respond to pressure, stretch or vibration, including Meissner corpuscles, Pacinian corpuscles, Merkel disks, Ruffini corpuscles and Golgi tendon organs.
Chaotic, uncoordinated ventricular electrical activity with no effective pumping, causing cardiac arrest. Treated with immediate defibrillation.
Disease of many peripheral nerves at once, typically causing symmetric distal sensory loss and weakness in a stocking-glove pattern. Common causes are diabetes, alcohol and Guillain-Barre syndrome.
The artery supplying the arm, branching off the brachiocephalic trunk on the right and arching directly from the aorta on the left. Becomes the axillary artery at the first rib.
Predictable exertional chest pain from fixed coronary narrowing that resolves with rest or nitroglycerin, without ST elevation or troponin rise.
The spectrum of acute myocardial ischemia from plaque rupture with thrombosis: unstable angina, NSTEMI and STEMI.
Abnormally elevated blood lipids (cholesterol, triglycerides or both), increasing atherosclerosis risk; severe hypertriglyceridemia can cause pancreatitis.
The change in lung volume per unit change in pressure; a measure of lung distensibility. Decreased in pulmonary fibrosis and increased in emphysema.
The pressure exerted by one gas in a mixture, proportional to its fraction of the total (Dalton law). Gas moves between alveoli and blood down partial pressure gradients.
The protein component of hemoglobin or myoglobin. Adult hemoglobin has two alpha and two beta globin chains; defects cause thalassemia and sickle cell disease.
Excessive saliva or drooling, due to impaired swallowing or increased production. Seen in Parkinson disease, ALS, esophageal atresia and cholinergic excess.
A nontuberculous mycobacterium (M. avium complex) causing disseminated infection in AIDS patients with CD4 below 50. Prophylaxis is with azithromycin.

A genus of blood flukes acquired by skin contact with freshwater containing snail-borne cercariae. S. mansoni and japonicum cause hepatosplenic disease; S. haematobium causes hematuria and bladder cancer.
Elevated blood insulin, seen in insulin resistance, obesity and insulinoma, and can cause hypoglycemia.
Immature granulocyte precursors in the bone marrow. The sequence runs myeloblast, promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band cell, then mature neutrophil.

Autosomal recessive defect in galactose metabolism, most often galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency, causing failure to thrive, jaundice, cataracts and E. coli sepsis in infants fed milk.
A small organic non-protein molecule (often a vitamin derivative such as NAD or CoA) that binds an enzyme to help it carry out a reaction.
A toxic alcohol in antifreeze that is metabolized to oxalic acid, causing anion gap metabolic acidosis and calcium oxalate crystals in urine with renal failure. Treated with fomepizole.
Drugs that suppress uterine contractions to delay preterm labor, such as nifedipine, terbutaline and indomethacin.
An alpha-1 agonist causing vasoconstriction, used to raise blood pressure, as a decongestant and for mydriasis without cycloplegia. Can cause reflex bradycardia.
A loop diuretic that inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb. Used in edema and heart failure; causes hypokalemia, ototoxicity and hypocalcemia.
A technique using fluorescent-labeled antibodies to detect antigens or antibodies in tissue, used for example to show immune deposits in glomerulonephritis and blistering skin disease.
A B-cell lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma producing monoclonal IgM, causing hyperviscosity (blurred vision, bleeding, neurologic symptoms) without lytic bone lesions.

Glomerular disease with subepithelial immune complex deposits causing diffuse basement membrane thickening and nephrotic syndrome. Often due to anti-PLA2R antibodies, and also hepatitis B, lupus and drugs.
A superficial, contagious skin infection by S. aureus or S. pyogenes, producing honey-colored crusted lesions, mainly in children. Bullous impetigo is toxin-mediated.
The muscles and fascia (levator ani and coccygeus) that support the pelvic organs. Weakness leads to prolapse and incontinence.
Nerve damage from chronic hyperglycemia, causing symmetric distal sensory loss, pain and autonomic dysfunction such as gastroparesis and orthostatic hypotension.
The middle part of the small intestine between the duodenum and ileum, with tall circular folds and long villi; the main site of nutrient absorption.
Anemia with enlarged red cells (MCV above 100). Megaloblastic causes are B12 and folate deficiency; non-megaloblastic causes include alcohol, liver disease and hypothyroidism.

Acquired stem cell disorder (PIGA mutation) lacking GPI-anchored complement inhibitors CD55 and CD59, causing complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis with hemoglobinuria and thrombosis. Treated with eculizumab.

Test for antibodies on red cells. The direct test detects antibody bound to a patient's red cells (autoimmune hemolysis); the indirect test detects serum antibodies against red cell antigens (crossmatching).
Slurred, poorly articulated speech due to weakness or incoordination of the muscles of speech. Cerebellar disease causes scanning (staccato) speech.
Neurologic conditions causing abnormal or excessive movement, such as Parkinson disease, chorea, dystonia, tremor and tics, usually from basal ganglia dysfunction.
G-protein-coupled receptors (mu, delta, kappa) binding endogenous endorphins and opioid drugs. Mu receptor activation causes analgesia, respiratory depression and constipation.
Degeneration of the macula causing loss of central vision. The dry form shows drusen and atrophy; the wet form involves choroidal neovascularization and is treated with anti-VEGF injections.

A flavivirus spread by Aedes mosquitoes, causing high fever, severe muscle and joint pain (breakbone fever), rash and thrombocytopenia. A second infection with a different serotype risks hemorrhagic fever.
A thread used to close wounds; also a fibrous joint between skull bones (cranial sutures).
Replacement of the lower esophageal squamous epithelium with intestinal-type columnar epithelium containing goblet cells, from chronic acid reflux. Predisposes to esophageal adenocarcinoma.
A comma-shaped, oxidase-positive gram-negative rod causing cholera. Its toxin activates Gs, increasing cAMP and causing profuse rice-water diarrhea.
Jaundice from blocked bile flow (gallstone, pancreatic head cancer, stricture), giving conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, pale stools, dark urine, pruritus and elevated alkaline phosphatase.
Gallbladder inflammation, usually from a stone blocking the cystic duct. Presents with right upper quadrant pain, fever and a positive Murphy sign.
A condition of many vascular lesions or proliferating blood vessels. Bacillary angiomatosis, caused by Bartonella in AIDS patients, produces red vascular skin papules.
Swollen vascular cushions in the anal canal. Internal hemorrhoids (above the dentate line) are painless and bleed; external ones (below it) can be painful when thrombosed.
A tear in the anal mucosa, usually posterior midline, causing painful defecation with bright red blood. Chronic cases are linked to sphincter spasm; Crohn disease is a cause of lateral fissures.
A live vaccine made from a weakened pathogen, giving strong, durable immunity but contraindicated in immunocompromised patients and pregnancy. Examples are MMR, varicella and oral polio.
Autoimmune blistering disease with IgG against desmoglein 3, causing flaccid intraepidermal bullae with oral erosions, a positive Nikolsky sign and a net-like immunofluorescence pattern.
An oral antifungal that binds microtubules, inhibiting mitosis, and is deposited in keratin. Used for dermatophyte infections of hair and nails; induces cytochrome P450 and is teratogenic.
A gram-negative coccobacillus with bipolar (safety-pin) staining that causes plague. Transmitted by fleas from rodents, producing painful lymph node buboes.
An encapsulated, spore-forming gram-positive rod that causes anthrax. Its toxin (edema factor, protective antigen, lethal factor) causes black eschar skin lesions or hemorrhagic mediastinitis.
The amount of virus in blood, measured by quantitative PCR (e.g., HIV RNA copies/mL). Used to monitor disease activity and treatment response.
A family of enveloped, single-stranded RNA viruses carried by rodents, causing Lassa fever and lymphocytic choriomeningitis. Particles contain ribosome-like granules giving a sandy appearance.
Fifth disease, caused by parvovirus B19, with bright red "slapped cheek" rash then a lacy body rash. It infects red cell precursors, causing aplastic crisis in sickle cell patients.
DNA and RNA, polymers of nucleotides linked by phosphodiester bonds that store and transmit genetic information.
An enzyme that splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide. Produced by H. pylori, Proteus, Cryptococcus and Ureaplasma; raises pH and promotes struvite stones.
The smallest amino acid, abundant in collagen and used in heme and creatine synthesis. Acts as an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord and brainstem.
A genus of gram-negative enteric rods that are lactose fermenters, causing hospital-acquired urinary and bloodstream infections, often with inducible AmpC beta-lactamase.
A gram-negative enteric rod producing a red pigment, causing hospital-acquired infections of the urinary tract, wounds and lungs.
The viscous fluid in joint cavities that lubricates and nourishes cartilage. Analysis helps diagnose septic arthritis, gout (needle crystals) and pseudogout (rhomboid crystals).
A sulfone antibiotic that inhibits folate synthesis, used for leprosy and Pneumocystis prophylaxis. Causes hemolysis in G6PD deficiency and methemoglobinemia.
The protein shell that encloses a virus's genetic material, built from repeating subunits (capsomeres).
Excess prolactin, commonly from a pituitary prolactinoma, dopamine antagonists or hypothyroidism. Causes galactorrhea, amenorrhea and infertility; treated with cabergoline.
The genetic makeup of an individual, i.e., the alleles carried at a locus, as opposed to the observable trait (phenotype).
A nitrogenous base (purine or pyrimidine) attached to a sugar but without phosphate. Nucleoside analogs, such as acyclovir and zidovudine, are antiviral drugs that terminate DNA chains.

The process in the seminiferous tubules by which spermatogonia develop into mature sperm, taking about 2 months and requiring testosterone and FSH. Spermiogenesis is the final differentiation of spermatids into sperm.
The organelle that modifies, sorts and packages proteins and lipids, adding glycosylation (including mannose-6-phosphate to lysosomal enzymes) before dispatch.
The mitochondrial enzyme (P450scc) that converts cholesterol to pregnenolone, the rate-limiting step of steroid hormone synthesis.
Enzymes in steroid synthesis that interconvert hydroxyl and keto groups, e.g., 3-beta-HSD converts pregnenolone to progesterone, and 17-beta-HSD makes testosterone and estradiol.
Cushing syndrome caused specifically by an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma. Features high ACTH, bilateral adrenal hyperplasia and cortisol suppression with high-dose dexamethasone.
Backward flow of menstrual blood through the fallopian tubes into the pelvis; a proposed cause of endometriosis.
Clusters of endocrine cells in the pancreas: alpha cells secrete glucagon, beta cells insulin, delta cells somatostatin. Beta cells are the most numerous, in the center.
A benign suprasellar tumor from Rathke pouch remnants. Presents in children with bitemporal hemianopsia and hypopituitarism, with calcifications on imaging.
An incretin hormone released by intestinal L cells after meals that enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion and slows gastric emptying. GLP-1 agonists (exenatide, liraglutide) treat diabetes.
Oral diabetes drugs (pioglitazone, rosiglitazone) that activate PPAR-gamma, increasing insulin sensitivity. Cause weight gain, edema and heart failure risk.
Female germ cells. Primary oocytes arrest in prophase I from fetal life until ovulation; the secondary oocyte arrests in metaphase II until fertilization.
Trisomy 18, causing severe intellectual disability, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, micrognathia and heart defects. Most die within the first year.
The thick smooth muscle layer of the uterine wall, which contracts in labor and bleeds after delivery when atonic.

Cytoskeletal proteins of intermediate thickness providing structural strength, with cell-type-specific forms: keratin (epithelium), vimentin (mesenchyme), desmin (muscle), GFAP (astrocytes), neurofilaments (neurons) and lamins.
A numerical or structural change in chromosomes, such as aneuploidy (trisomy 21), deletions, translocations and inversions.
The number of pregnancies carried beyond viability. Nulliparity means never having given birth and multiparity means having had more than one birth.
Four paired nuclei deep in the cerebellum (lateral to medial: dentate, emboliform, globose, fastigial) that provide output to the brainstem and thalamus.
Death of fat cells. In the breast, it follows trauma and forms a firm lump that mimics cancer; in pancreatitis, enzymatic fat necrosis forms calcium soaps.
A placental protein measured in first-trimester screening; low levels suggest increased risk of Down syndrome.
Addition of a methyl group to a molecule. Methylation of cytosine in DNA silences genes, and methylation of histones regulates chromatin.
Two-ring nitrogenous bases (adenine and guanine); degraded to uric acid, which accumulates in gout.
X-linked recessive dystrophin gene mutation (frameshift) causing progressive muscle weakness, calf pseudohypertrophy and Gowers sign. Becker dystrophy is a milder in-frame variant.
A cardiac muscle cell; striated, branched, usually with one central nucleus, joined end to end by intercalated discs with gap junctions and desmosomes.
Inherited deficiencies of lysosomal enzymes, causing buildup of undegraded substrates. Examples are Gaucher, Tay-Sachs, Fabry, Niemann-Pick and Hurler.
A stretchy connective tissue protein rich in glycine and proline, found in lungs, skin and arteries; cross-linked by lysyl oxidase. Broken down by elastase, which alpha-1-antitrypsin inhibits.
Mitochondrial ATP production in which electrons pass down the electron transport chain, pumping protons out; ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP.
Autosomal dominant NF1 mutation causing neurofibromas, cafe-au-lait spots, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules and optic gliomas. Also called von Recklinghausen disease.

Positive predictive value is the probability that a patient with a positive test truly has the disease; negative predictive value is the probability that a negative result truly means no disease. Both depend on prevalence.
A rapid wide-complex rhythm of at least three beats arising from the ventricles, usually in structural heart disease. Can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation.
A non-striated muscle cell in hollow organs and vessel walls; contracts via calcium-calmodulin activating myosin light chain kinase.
Alpha-hemolytic, optochin-resistant streptococci of the oral flora that cause dental caries and subacute bacterial endocarditis on damaged valves after dental procedures.
A combined alpha-1 and non-selective beta blocker used for hypertensive emergencies and hypertension in pregnancy.
Cholesterol with a fatty acid attached, formed by LCAT in plasma and ACAT in cells. It is the storage form of cholesterol and fills the core of lipoproteins.
Lipid-lowering drugs (gemfibrozil, fenofibrate) that activate PPAR-alpha, mainly lowering triglycerides. Cause myopathy and gallstones.
An enzyme on capillary endothelium that breaks down triglycerides in chylomicrons and VLDL, activated by apolipoprotein C-II. Deficiency causes hypertriglyceridemia.
A gram-negative rod that grows on charcoal yeast agar with iron and cysteine, causing Legionnaires disease (pneumonia with diarrhea and hyponatremia) from contaminated water systems.
Red cell destruction by autoantibodies. Warm type (IgG, extravascular, with lupus) and cold agglutinin disease (IgM, with Mycoplasma and EBV) are the main forms.
CD4 helper T cells driven by IL-12 that secrete interferon-gamma, activating macrophages and fighting intracellular pathogens.
A free-living amoeba (N. fowleri) from warm fresh water that enters through the cribriform plate, causing rapidly fatal primary amebic meningoencephalitis.
A protein in neuroendocrine secretory granules; a tumor marker for neuroendocrine tumors such as carcinoid and pheochromocytoma.
Cells that receive neural input and release hormones, such as enterochromaffin cells, adrenal chromaffin cells and pancreatic islet cells. Tumors express chromogranin and synaptophysin.
Direct visualization of the airways with a flexible scope, used to biopsy lesions, remove foreign bodies and obtain lavage samples.
A coagulation factor, cofactor for converting prothrombin to thrombin. The factor V Leiden mutation resists inactivation by activated protein C and causes hereditary thrombophilia.
The inactive precursor of plasmin, the enzyme that dissolves fibrin clots. Activated by tPA, which is given therapeutically in stroke and MI.
A nonpolar amino acid; carries amino groups from muscle to liver in the glucose-alanine cycle and is the substrate for ALT.
The brush-border enzyme that splits lactose into glucose and galactose. Deficiency causes lactose intolerance with bloating and watery diarrhea after dairy.
Prostaglandin I2, made by endothelium, which dilates vessels and inhibits platelet aggregation. Epoprostenol is used for pulmonary hypertension.
Excessive daytime sleepiness despite adequate sleep, seen in narcolepsy, sleep apnea and idiopathic hypersomnia.
Abnormal connection between trachea and esophagus. The most common type has proximal esophageal atresia and distal fistula, causing drooling, choking and aspiration with feeding.
Protrusion of abdominal organs into the chest through a diaphragm defect. The congenital form (usually left posterolateral, Bochdalek) causes pulmonary hypoplasia.
Drugs that widen airways: beta-2 agonists (albuterol), anticholinergics (ipratropium) and methylxanthines (theophylline), used in asthma and COPD.
The enzyme converting hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid. Inhibited by allopurinol and febuxostat in gout.
An alkylating chemotherapy agent related to cyclophosphamide that causes hemorrhagic cystitis, prevented with mesna.
An immunosuppressant that binds cyclophilin and inhibits calcineurin, blocking IL-2 transcription and T-cell activation. Causes nephrotoxicity, hypertension and gingival hyperplasia.
A non-protein amino acid in the urea cycle; ornithine transcarbamylase combines it with carbamoyl phosphate to make citrulline. Deficiency causes hyperammonemia with orotic aciduria.

Autosomal recessive phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency (or BH4 defect) causing phenylalanine accumulation, intellectual disability, musty odor and fair skin. Treated with low-phenylalanine diet; tyrosine becomes essential.
The enzyme converting dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate, needed for thymidine synthesis. Inhibited by methotrexate, trimethoprim and pyrimethamine.
Enzymes that break down acetylcholine (acetylcholinesterase at synapses; pseudocholinesterase in plasma). Inhibited by organophosphates and drugs like neostigmine.
A neurologic disorder of multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic starting before age 18, often with OCD or ADHD. Treated with antipsychotics or alpha-2 agonists.
Psychiatric disorder after trauma with intrusive memories, avoidance, negative mood and hyperarousal lasting more than a month. Treated with SSRIs and trauma-focused therapy.
An antiepileptic that blocks sodium channels and enhances GABA, used for seizures and migraine prevention. Causes kidney stones, weight loss and cognitive slowing; teratogenic.
Test for hidden blood in stool, used to screen for colorectal cancer or detect GI bleeding.
The malaria parasite causing the most severe disease, with ring forms and banana-shaped gametocytes and high parasitemia. Infected cells stick to vessels, causing cerebral malaria.
White blood cells with cytoplasmic granules: neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils.
The midline ventricle between the two halves of the thalamus, connected to the lateral ventricles by the foramina of Monro and the fourth ventricle by the cerebral aqueduct.
The area of frontal cortex (precentral gyrus, Brodmann area 4) whose neurons send voluntary movement commands via the corticospinal tract, arranged somatotopically.
Tertiary syphilis affecting the dorsal columns and roots, causing impaired proprioception, wide-based ataxia, lancinating pain and Argyll Robertson pupils.

The artery ascending through the cervical transverse foramina and joining its partner to form the basilar artery; supplies the brainstem and cerebellum. Dissection can cause posterior circulation stroke.
Clonal bone marrow disorders with ineffective hematopoiesis, causing cytopenias and dysplastic cells (such as pseudo-Pelger-Huet cells), with risk of progression to acute myeloid leukemia.
A midbrain nucleus with dopaminergic, melanin-containing neurons projecting to the striatum. Degeneration of the pars compacta causes Parkinson disease.
The point where the optic nerve and retinal vessels exit the eye; it has no photoreceptors, creating the physiologic blind spot. Swelling indicates papilledema.
A vinca alkaloid that blocks microtubule assembly, arresting cells in metaphase. Used for Hodgkin lymphoma and testicular cancer; causes bone marrow suppression.
Colon inflammation from reduced blood flow, typically at watershed areas (splenic flexure), presenting with abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea in older adults. Imaging may show thumbprinting.
A high-potency typical antipsychotic blocking dopamine D2 receptors. Causes extrapyramidal effects (dystonia, parkinsonism), QT prolongation and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Group A strep pharyngitis with a pyrogenic exotoxin, causing a sandpaper-like body rash, strawberry tongue and Pastia lines.
Acute liver inflammation from heavy alcohol use, with jaundice, fever, AST greater than ALT (about 2:1) and Mallory bodies on biopsy.
A long-acting opioid agonist used for opioid withdrawal and maintenance therapy. Can prolong the QT interval.
An anticonvulsant binding alpha-2-delta subunits of voltage-gated calcium channels, used for neuropathic pain, postherpetic neuralgia and partial seizures. Causes sedation and ataxia.
A disease of the joints. Examples include Charcot arthropathy in neuropathy and hemophilic arthropathy.
A vaccine made from killed pathogens; safe in immunocompromised patients but less immunogenic, often needing boosters. Examples are IPV, hepatitis A and rabies.
A group of skin diseases with fine scaling, such as pityriasis rosea (herald patch then Christmas-tree rash) and pityriasis versicolor (Malassezia).
The part of the pharynx behind the mouth, between the soft palate and the epiglottis, containing the tonsils.
